The [[Aztec]]s gathered the wild plant as well as cultivating it for medicinal, ceremonial and decorative purposes; it was introduced to Europe after the [[Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire|Spanish conquest]] of the [[Aztec Empire]] and colonization{{cite journal |last1=López Estrada |first1=Daniel |last2=Chang |first2=Wen-Te |last3=Heinrich |first3=Michael |title=From "traditional" to modern medicine: A medical and historical analysis of Tagetes erecta L. (Cempasúchil) |journal=Journal of Traditional and Complementary Medicine |url=https://pdf.sciencedirectassets.com/312078/1-s2.0-S2225411024X00073/1-s2.0-S2225411024000920/main.pdf |date=January 2025 |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=6–14 |doi=10.1016/j.jtcme.2024.08.001 }}{{rp|7}} and became widely cultivated commercially with many [[cultivar]]s in use as [[ornamental plant]]s,{{cite web |date=2003 |last=Evans |first=Erv |url=http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/depts/hort/consumer/factsheets/annuals/tagetes_erecta.html |title=Annual Flowers: ''Tagetes erecta'', ''T. patula'' |website=NC State Horticulture trade.[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200024576 Flora of China, ''Tagetes erecta'' Linnaeus, 1753. 万寿菊 wan shou ju ][http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=tagetes+erecta Altervista Flora Italiana, Tagete eretta, ''Tagetes erecta'' L.] Some authorities regard ''[[Tagetes patula]]'' (the French marigold) as a [[synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] of ''Tagetes erecta''.{{cite web | url= http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/gcc-137312 | title= ''Tagetes patula'' | publisher= The Plant List | access-date = 1 December 2018}} == Names == The Spanish name ''{{lang|es|cempazúchitl}}'' (or ''{{lang|es|cempasúchil}}'') comes from the [[Nahuatl language|Nahuatl]] ''{{lang|nah|cempohualxochitl}}'' ("[[20 (number)|twenty]] flower"){{cite web |title=Day of the Dead Flowers |url=https://www.mexican-folk-art-guide.com/day-of-the-dead-flowers.html#.Xoe-SohKjIU |website=Copal, Mexican Folk Art at its best Online. |access-date=3 April 2020 |archive-date=1 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221101014650/https://www.mexican-folk-art-guide.com/day-of-the-dead-flowers.html#.Xoe-SohKjIU |url-status=dead }} – 20 (''{{lang|nah|cempohualli}}'') is the base of the Aztec [[vigesimal]] counting system, consequently a symbol of completion including in life reflected in measurements like [[Aztec calendar#Tōnalpōhualli|their calendrical daycount]].{{rp|12}} The English name ''marigold'' comes from their petals' arrangement resembling ''[[Calendula officinalis]]'', also called "Mary's gold" or "marigold".{{cite web |last1=Perez |first1=Julio |date=26 October 2023 |title=Marigolds: Blooms of Cultural Significance |url=https://blogs.ifas.ufl.edu/putnamco/2023/10/26/marigolds-blooms-of-cultural-significance/ |website=Putnam County |publisher=[[University of Florida]] [[Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences]] |access-date=1 May 2025 }} In [[Thai language|Thai]], it is called {{lang|th|ดาวเรือง}} ''daao reuaang'' meaning "glittering star".{{cite journal |last1=Xu |first1=Li-Wei |last2=Wang |first2=Guo-Ying |last3=Yan-Ping |first3=Shi |s2cid=38292218 |journal=Chemistry of Natural Compounds |title=Chemical constituents from ''Tagetes erecta'' flowers |date=May 2011 |volume=47 |issue=2 |pages=81–283 |doi=10.1007/s10600-011-9905-5}} ==Description== It is a [[herbaceous]] [[annual plant|annual]] or [[perennial plant]] whose height ranges from 30 to 110 cm. The root is cylindrical, pivoting, with a [[fibrous]] and shallow [[branch]]ing system. The stem is striated, sometimes ridged, smooth or slightly with villi, cylindrical, oval and herbaceous to slightly woody, with [[resin]] channels in the bark, which are [[aromatic]] when squeezed. Opposite leaves at the bottom alternate at the top, up to 20 cm long, pinnate, composed of 11 to 17 leaflets, [[lanceolate]] to linear-lanceolate, up to 5 cm long and 1.5 cm wide, acute to acuminate, serrated to sub-holders, the lower ones of each leaf frequently setiform (in the form of threads), the superiors are sometimes completely setiform; with abundant round glands.{{cite book |last1= Rzedowski |first1= J. |last2= Rzedowski |first2= G.C. |year= 2005|title= Fanerogamic Flora of the Valley of Mexico |volume = II |edition= 1st |location= Mexico City |publisher= National School of Biological Sciences, IPN, Institute of Biology }} The main characteristic of the flowers is that they are grouped in small heads or in solitary [[inflorescence]]s, on [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]] up to 15 cm long, they are liguladas of yellow colors to red. In the flowers of the disc: 150 to 250 in the simple heads, in the doubles it shows different degrees of transformation in [[ligules]], yellow to orange [[Corolla (botany)|corolla]]s, of 8 to 10 mm in length. The fruits and seeds are: linear achenes 7 to 10 mm long, smooth or slightly covered with stiff hairs at the corners. It has a long flowering period extending throughout the summer and fall. It reproduces easily by seeds.{{cite journal |last1= Vázquez-García |first1= L. M. |last2= Víveros-Farfán |first2= I. M. G. |last3= Salomé-Castañeda |first3= E. |year= 2002 |title= Cempasúchil (''Tagetes'' spp.) |journal= Ornamental Phytogenetic Resources of Mexico |publisher= University of the State of Mexico |pages= 28–67 }} ==Distribution and habitat== Although native to Mexico, they are also found in the countries of [[Central America]] and the [[Caribbean]]: Belize, Bolivia, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Guyana, Honduras, Jamaica, Nicaragua, Panama, Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic and Venezuela.{{cite book |last1= Villaseñor |first1= R. |last2= Espinosa G. |first2= J. L. |last3= Espinosa G. | first3= F. J. |year= 1998 |title= Catalog of weeds of Mexico |location= Mexico City |publisher= National Autonomous University of Mexico, National Consultative Phytosanitary Council, Fund of Economic Culture |page= |isbn=}} In their wild form they are found in the Balsas basin and western Mexico and live in diverse types of ecosystems, such as tropical deciduous forests, thorny forests, cloud forests and pine-oak forests. In the wild, it is found as a getaway in heavily disturbed places at altitudes of 800–2300 m.{{cite conference |url= |title= |last1= Heyden |first1= Doris |author-link1= |last2= |first2= |author-link2= |date= 1987 |orig-date= 8 and 9 October 1983 |publisher= |book-title= Symbolism of ceramics from the Templo Mayor |pages= |location= Dumbarton Oaks |conference= The Aztec Templo Mayor: A Symposium at Dumbarton Oaks|isbn=9780884021490}} As an introduced species (cultivated) it can be found in China, India, Zambia, Zimbabwe, South Africa and Australia. ==History== [[File:Gc31 tagetes erecta and patula.jpg|thumb|220px|Botanical illustration.]] The archaeological record of the use of ''Tagetes erecta'' among pre-Hispanic civilizations is not as abundant as in the case of other species of the same family. For example, it has been possible to establish the ceremonial use among the [[Mexica]] of ''[[Tagetes lucida|T. lucida]]'' as an aromatic plant, which they called yauhtli, through the chemical analysis of the incense burners found in the remains of the [[Templo Mayor]] in Mexico City.{{Cite web |date=2016-03-13 |title=Humo aromático para los dioses |language=es |url=http://www.mesoweb.com/about/articles/Humo.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160313072247/http://www.mesoweb.com/about/articles/Humo.pdf |archive-date=2016-03-13 |access-date=2023-04-15 }} The [[Nahuatl]] term cempoalxóchitl, was used to refer to several species of flowers, which includes ''T. erecta'', ''T. lucida'', ''[[Tagetes patula|T. patula]]'', ''[[Tagetes lunulata|T. lunulata]]'', ''[[Tagetes tenuifolia|T. tenuifolia]]'', ''[[Tagetes peduncularis|T. peduncularis]]'' and ''[[Tagetes elongata|T. elongata]]''. This complicates the differentiation of one species and another when such a term is used, however, it appears that ''T. erecta'' was primarily named by this term. The identification of ''T. erecta'' as some flowers represented in Aztec art, such as those seen in the [[Coyolxāuhqui|Coyolxauhqui]] monolith, as part of the goddess's headdress, has been proposed as a symbol of her sovereignty or her death. They are part of the necklace that a plant deity wears in a vase found in the Templo Mayor, although it could also be ''T. patula''. With the arrival of the [[Spaniards]] in Mexico, the documentary record of the ceremonial and medicinal use of ''T. erecta'' increased in which the flower is described by [[Bernardino de Sahagún]] as:{{cite book |last1= Jäger |first1= Eckehart J.|last2= Ebel |first2= Friedrich |last3= Hanelt |first3= Peter |editor-last1= Müller| editor-first1= Gerd K. |year= 2008 |title= Excursion flora of Germany. Founded by Werner Rothmaler. |volume= 5 : Herbaceous ornamental and useful plants |location= Berlin / Heidelberg |publisher= Springer, Spektrum Academic Publisher |page= 603 |isbn=978-3-8274-0918-8}}
These flowers are called ''Cempoalxóchitl''; they are yellow and of good smell, and wide and beautiful, that they are born, and others that sow them in the orchards; They are in two ways, some they call females ''Cempoalxóchitl'' and they are big and beautiful, and others that are called ''Cempoalxóchitl'' males are not so beautiful or so big.
Sahagún also describes, in the same work, that the plant had a role in the rituals of the religious Mexica festival in the [[Aztec calendar#Veintenas of the xiuhpōhualli|month]] of ''Teculhuitontli'', where the goddess of salt ''Huixtocíhuatl'', whose color was yellow, was celebrated and who offered herself as sacrifice a woman. In the work of the physician [[Francisco Hernández de Toledo|Francisco Hernández]], it is described that the name ''cempoalxóchitl'' received at least seven types of flowers, noting that the term properly described the largest of them and that the Spaniards called it carnation of Indian, also lists its medical properties.Serrato-Cruz M. A. 2005. Collection, characterization and use of ''Tagetes erecta'' L. As ornamental; Advances X National Congress and III International Ornamental Horticulture. Michoacán University of San Nicolás de Hidalgo. Michoacán, Mexico ==Cultivation== It is widely cultivated and there are many [[cultivars]] used in gardening as an [[ornamental plant]]. The cultivar 'Inca Orange' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/176840/i-Tagetes-erecta-i-Inca-Orange-(Inca-Series)/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder – ''Tagetes'' 'Inca Orange' | access-date = 1 December 2018}}{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants – Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 100 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 1 December 2018}} In Mexico, it is used in the festivities of the [[Day of the Dead]], to decorate altars and tombs; hence the name "flower of the dead". However, since antiquity it is also used for food and medicinal purposes. ==Uses== ===Rituals=== The meaning of the flower's name to the Aztecs makes the ''cempasúchil'' symbolic and used in the {{lang|es|[[Día de Muertos]]}} celebration every 2 November in Mexico, it is also called the ''{{lang|es|flor de muertos}}'' ("flower of the dead").{{cite web |title=Marigold: the typical flower to celebrate the Day of The Dead |url=https://www.floraldaily.com/article/9130021/marigold-the-typical-flower-to-celebrate-the-day-of-the-dead/ |website=www.floraldaily.com |access-date=3 April 2020 |language=EN}} Water infused with its fragrant [[essential oil]] is used to wash [[Cadaver|corpses]] in [[Honduras]], and the flower is still commonly planted in [[cemetery|cemeteries]].{{cite web |url=http://database.prota.org/dbtw-wpd/exec/dbtwpub.dll?AC=QBE_QUERY&BU=http://database.prota.org/search.htm&TN=PROTAB~1&QB0=AND&QF0=Species+Code&QI0=Tagetes+erecta&RF=Webdisplay |title=''Tagetes erecta'' |publisher=Protabase |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171018072012/http://database.prota.org/dbtw-wpd/exec/dbtwpub.dll?AC=QBE_QUERY&BU=http%3A%2F%2Fdatabase.prota.org%2Fsearch.htm&TN=PROTAB~1&QB0=AND&QF0=Species+Code&QI0=Tagetes+erecta&RF=Webdisplay |archive-date=2017-10-18 }} ===Medicine=== Since [[prehispanic]] times, this plant has been used for medicinal purposes.{{Cite web |title=Mexican marigold {{!}} Kew |url=https://www.kew.org/plants/mexican-marigold |access-date=2024-05-07 |website=www.kew.org}} The [[Cherokee]] used it as a skin wash and for yellow dye.[http://herb.umd.umich.edu/herb/search.pl?searchstring=Tagetes+erecta Ethnobotany] The pigments of the erect tagetes are due to the presence of [[carotenoids]], of which the main one is [[lutein]], which is associated with the prevention of the development of age-related [[eye disease]]s such as [[cataracts]] and [[macular degeneration]]. The most intense orange tones of the flowers are related to a higher content of carotenoids, especially xanthophyll. Some studies indicate the effectiveness of the latter in the prevention of [[coronary artery disease]], [[heart attack]]s, immune response, old age and [[cancer]]. In some regions of Mexico it is used in [[Digestion|digestive]] [[ailment]]s, such as [[stomach pain]], as well as [[diarrhea]], [[colic]], liver problems, [[bile]], [[vomiting]], and [[indigestion]]. The plant also has a history of use against [[intestinal parasite]]s and worms with one study indicating that it has a different mechanism than the anthelmintic drug [[levamisole]].{{cite journal |last1=Piña-Vázquez |first1=DM |last2=Mayoral-Peña |first2=Z |last3=Gómez-Sánchez |first3=M |last4=Salazar-Olivo |first4=LA |last5=Arellano-Carbajal |first5=F |title=Anthelmintic effect of Psidium guajava and Tagetes erecta on wild-type and Levamisole-resistant Caenorhabditis elegans strains. |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |date=18 April 2017 |volume=202 |pages=92–96 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2017.03.004 |pmid=28286043}} Other uses include respiratory diseases such as colds, [[flu]], [[bronchitis]] and [[nasal congestion]] as well as [[gynecological]] problems.E. Prinz: "Dyeing plants - Instructions for dyeing, use in culture and medicine" Verlag Schweizerbart, Stuttgart 2009, {{ISBN|978-3-510-65258-7}}, p 53. Antioxidant activity has been discovered in the [[essential oil]] of this plant although less than that of [[α-Tocopherol]], possibly attributable to the presence of [[camphor]] and [[methyl eugenol]].{{cite journal |author1=Olabiyi, T. I. |author2=E. E. A. Oyedunmade |name-list-style=amp | year = 2007 | url = http://www.acss.ws/Upload/XML/Research/389.pdf | title = Marigold (''Tagetes erecta'' L.) as interplant with cowpea for the control of nematode pests | journal = African Crop Science Conference Proceedings | volume = 8 | pages = 1075–1078}} It is most effective against the nematode species ''[[Pratylenchus penetrans]]''. ===Culinary=== The ray florets have been used in [[salad|lettuce salads]] and other foods to add colour and flavour. The flowers are rich in carotenoids, and are thus used to make food and feed pigments.Heuzé V., Tran G., Hassoun P., Lebas F., 2017. Mexican marigold (Tagetes erecta). Feedipedia, a programme by INRA, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO. https://www.feedipedia.org/node/90 Last updated on August 24, 2017, 15:11 The dried flower petals, ground to a powder, are used in poultry feed to ensure a good colouration of [[egg yolk]]s and broiler skin, especially in the absence of well-pigmented [[Corn|yellow maize]] in the feed.{{cite journal |author=W. Leigh Hadden |author2=Ruth H. Watkins |author3=Luis W. Levy |author4=Edmundo Regalado |author5=Diana M. Rivadeneira |author6=Richard B. van Breemen |author7=Steven J. It is also used to enhance colouring in [[crustacean]]s, such as the [[Whiteleg shrimp|Pacific white shrimp]] (''Litopenaeus vannamei'').{{cite journal |author=J. T. Ponce-Palafox |author2=J. L.
